'''''Poa infirma''''', also known as '''early meadow-grass'''<ref name="BSBI07">{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> and '''weak bluegrass''', is a species of [[Poaceae|grass]] in the genus ''[[Poa]]''. It was first described in 1812 by German botanist  [[Carl Sigismund Kunth]] from a specimen found in [[Colombia]] between [[Fontibón]] and [[Santa Fe, Bogotá|Santa Fe]], in [[Bogotá|Bogota]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Kunth |title=Poa infirma |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/4821#page/221/mode/1up}}</ref> Despite this, it is actually [[introduced species|introduced]] in the Americas and is native to [[Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean]] [[Europe]], [[North Africa]] and [[West Asia]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Poa infirma Kunth, Nov. Gen. == Habitat ==
''P. infirma'' is typically a coastal species, found in open, trampled grassland, on cliff-tops, tracksides, picnic sites, lawns, and car parks, as well as in stabilised dunes.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Early Meadow-grass {{!}} NatureSpot |url=https://www.naturespot.org/species/early-meadow-grass |access-date=2026-08-25 |website=www.naturespot.org}}</ref>

It can also be found inland, typically in man-made habitats with poor or sand. It is often found in pavement cracks, depressions on eroded concrete, or on gravelly substrate on edges of car parks, roads, or industrial estates.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Early Meadow-grass identification |url=https://bsbi.org/learn/resources/identification-guides/early-meadow-grass-identification |access-date=2026-08-25 |website=Botanical Society of Britain & Ireland |language=en}}</ref>

== Distribution ==
''P. infirma'' is native to [[Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean]] [[Europe]], [[North Africa]] and [[West Asia]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> 

It is introduced on most continents: 

* [[Sub-Saharan Africa]]: [[Namibia]] and [[South Africa]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Soreng |first=Robert J. |last2=Sylvester |first2=Steven P. |last3=Sylvester |first3=Mitsy D. P. V. |last4=Clark |first4=Vincent Ralph |date=2020-10-28 |title=New records and key to Poa (Pooideae, Poaceae) from the Flora of Southern Africa region and notes on taxa including a diclinous breeding system in Poa binata |url=https://phytokeys.pensoft.net/article/55948/ |journal=PhytoKeys |language=en |volume=165 |pages=27–50 |doi=10.3897/phytokeys.165.55948  |doi-access=free|issn=1314-2003 |pmc=7642159 |pmid=33192144}}</ref>
* [[Australasia]]: [[New Zealand]] and [[Australia]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Poa infirma Australia |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Poa%20infirma}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Connor |date=2000 |title=Poa infirma New Zealand |url=https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/e4d29c3c-19cd-4487-a543-c642d512c241}}</ref>
* [[North America]]: Western coastline, including [[British Columbia]], [[Washington (state)|Washington]], [[Oregon]], [[California]], and [[Baja California]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Occurrence search |url=https://www.gbif.org/occurrence/search |access-date=2026-08-26 |website=www.gbif.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Please verify |url=https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi/auth/challenge?return_to=/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=38835 |access-date=2026-08-26 |website=ucjeps.berkeley.edu}}</ref>
* [[South America]]: [[Colombia]], [[Peru]], [[Bolivia]], [[Chile]], [[Argentina]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" />
It is unclear whether ''P. infirma'' is indigenous in China and Pakistan.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Poa infirma Pakistan |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=5&taxon_id=250034219}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Poa infirma China |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=250034219}}</ref>

In Britain, ''P. infirma'' has rapidly spread following human disturbance and climate change further north along the coast, as well as further inland.<ref name="BSBI07" />

== Identification ==
''P. infirma'' has two main forms: a small, densely tufted plant with short, compact inflorescences; and a lanky plant with tall, erect culms and spreading panicles. These forms apparently correspond to soil quality, with smaller plants typically growing in poorer soil. Its leaves are strikingly yellow-green.<ref name="BSBI07" /> 

It is very similar to ''[[Poa annua]]'', which is probably a daughter species.<ref name="grass">[http://herbarium.usu.edu/webmanual/info2.asp?name=Poa_infirma&type=treatment Grass Manual Treatment]</ref> The two species can be differentiated by ''P. infirma'' having much smaller anthers, elongated paleas, and a yellow-green colour.<ref>Chester, T. [http://tchester.org/plants/analysis/poa/annua_infirma.html Plants of Southern California: ''Poa annua'' and ''P. infirma'']</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
''Poa infirma'' was first described in 1812 by German botanist [[Carl Sigismund Kunth]] from a specimen found in [[Colombia]] between [[Fontibón]] and [[Santa Fe, Bogotá|Santa Fe]], in [[Bogotá|Bogota]].<ref name=":2" /> 

''Poa annua'' is an allotetraploid hybrid species that is derived from ''P. infirma'' and ''P. supina'' parents around 50,000 years ago.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Benson |first=Christopher W. |last2=Sheltra |first2=Matthew R. |last3=Maughan |first3=Peter J. |last4=Jellen |first4=Eric N. |last5=Robbins |first5=Matthew D. |last6=Bushman |first6=B. Shaun |last7=Patterson |first7=Eric L. |last8=Hall |first8=Nathan D. |last9=Huff |first9=David R. |date=2023-06-26 |title=Homoeologous evolution of the allotetraploid genome of Poa annua L |url=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10291818/ |journal=BMC genomics |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=350 |doi=10.1186/s12864-023-09456-5  |doi-access=free|issn=1471-2164 |pmc=10291818 |pmid=37365554}}</ref> ''P. annua'' and ''P. infirma'' are often confused and are believed to form a rare sterile hybrid.<ref name="grass" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Poa annua x infirma |url=https://bsbi.org/taxa/2cd4p9h.qrg/poa-annua-x-infirma}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Poa infirma – March 2020 – Somerset Rare Plants Group |url=https://www.somersetrareplantsgroup.org.uk/poa-infirma/ |access-date=2026-09-06 |language=en-GB}}</ref>
